title: Solidarity at the Gdansk Shipyard
text:
In August 1980 the management of the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk fired Anna Walentynowicz, a crane operator and independent union activist, a few months before she was due to retire. On 14 August the workers went on strike to demand her reinstatement and a pay rise. Lech Walesa, an electrician who had himself been fired for activism, climbed over the shipyard wall to join them and became the strike's leader.

Within two days management offered to meet the shipyard's demands, and Walesa announced that the strike was over. But workers from other factories and transport depots had walked out in support, and they feared they would be abandoned. Walentynowicz, Alina Pienkowska and other activists went to the gates and urged the shipyard workers to stay. Walesa reversed himself, and the strike continued as a solidarity strike.

Delegates from hundreds of workplaces formed an inter-factory strike committee in the shipyard and drew up a list of twenty-one demands, starting with the right to form free trade unions independent of the Communist Party. The gates were hung with flowers and pictures of the Pope, and the world's press gathered outside.

On 31 August the government signed the Gdansk Agreement, accepting independent unions for the first time in the Soviet bloc. Within months the new union, Solidarity, had about ten million members. It was banned under martial law in December 1981, but it survived underground and returned to lead Poland's peaceful transition in 1989.
lesson: A group is strongest when its members refuse to settle alone. Standing by the people who stood by you turns a local dispute into a movement.
people: Lech Walesa, Anna Walentynowicz, Alina Pienkowska, Gdansk shipyard workers
source: Gdansk Agreement (31 August 1980); Timothy Garton Ash, The Polish Revolution: Solidarity (1983)
